one_star_reviews.text:
I walked in with my own cups and asked if they charge for ice when we have our own cups as most places do not. The cashier looked like she was going to say no but a customer quickly spoke up as she was giving me dirty looks and said "no they charge". The gal at the register was on the phone but I could tell she was getting ready to answer and when the customer yelled that out, she kind of looked confused and went back to the call, neither confirming or denying the rude customers answer. Everyone inside the store continued to stare at me as if I didn't belong.  It was very strange because I grew up in Madera which is predominantly Hispanic and never felt as uncomfortable as I felt in this store. The customer especially who glared at me with a disgusted face. It was very obvious why.

Why am I holding that against the store itself?

The cashier was right there amd even though she was on the phone, she could have spoken up. She did not. So allowing that nasty type of behavior to go on is the same thing. If you're not actively against it, you're for it.

This is probably the first time I've ever left a review like this. Ive never experienced in ANY other establishment, including MANY Hispanic, even Spanish speaking ones. It was the nastiest feeling and then I felt like everyone outside was staring too. But as a psychologist, I know that I could have perceived it that way due to the encounter I had inside the store.

Overall the yuckiest place I've ever been to. Hate is ugly. I immediately stopped the pump which had been running into my gas tank, and decided it wasn't going to spend another penny there. Completely inappropriate and that behavior needs to get checked before it poisons the rest - if its not too late already. That was crazy.

Wow. Congratulations, my very first complaint over race. Way to go!

one_star_reviews.text: This is no longer the Valero they have a different name on the building

We rented this venue for my bridal shower, and unfortunately, our experience with the handling of the security deposit was extremely disappointing and, in our opinion, unfair.

The rental fee for the venue was $400, and we were additionally required to pay a $400 security deposit, meaning we paid $800 upfront. We understood that the $400 security deposit was refundable as long as the facility was left in acceptable condition.

My mother was responsible for cleaning the venue after our event. She swept and mopped the floor, cleaned up after the event, and made sure that all of our trash was completely removed from the property. We did not simply leave the venue as-is and walk away. We took the time to clean before leaving.

We also have photos and videos documenting the condition of the venue before, during, and after our event, including evidence of us cleaning. Importantly, the floor was already dirty when we arrived. We are not claiming the venue was spotless when we entered, because it was not. We made a genuine effort to leave the facility in a clean and reasonable condition.

Afterward, we received a message stating that only $350 of our $400 security deposit was being returned, meaning $50 was withheld. The explanation given was that two board members were “not happy with the condition  the floor was left in” and allegedly had to clean it themselves before their own function.

What is particularly frustrating is that we were not given any opportunity to address the issue before the deposit was partially withheld. If there was a specific problem with the floor, we would have appreciated being contacted and given the opportunity to discuss it or provide the documentation we have showing that the venue was cleaned.

The message also stated that the president, Christine, could be contacted if we wanted to question or dispute the deduction and that she had pictures. We absolutely intend to do so because we believe the situation deserves clarification.

The issue here is not simply the $50. It is the principle and the lack of transparency. When a venue requires a substantial security deposit, renters should be able to expect clear, consistent, and reasonable standards for determining whether that deposit is returned. If deductions are going to be made based on the opinion of board members, there should be clear documentation showing exactly what condition the facility was expected to be left in, what specific damage or cleaning was required, and why the amount withheld was justified.

We have our own documentation showing the condition of the facility and our efforts to clean it. The floor was dirty when we arrived, and we left it in a cleaned condition after sweeping and mopping. We also removed all of our trash from the property.

It is very disappointing to feel as though we did everything that was reasonably expected of us and still had part of our deposit withheld based on a subjective assessment after the fact.

For anyone considering renting this venue, I strongly recommend taking extensive photos and videos of the entire facility immediately upon arrival and again before leaving, including floors, bathrooms, kitchen areas, tables, chairs, and any other areas you are using. Document everything, because apparently the condition of the facility may later be judged differently by the board members.

I hope the management/board will review the situation fairly and consider the documentation we have. We rented the venue in good faith, paid the required fees, cleaned up after our event, removed our trash, and expected our refundable security deposit to be handled fairly.

This experience has left us very disappointed, especially because this was the venue for a special family celebration and bridal shower. The $50 is not the point — fair treatment, transparency, and accountability are.

one_star_reviews.text:
Very Disappointing Experience With Dr. Oefeleian

Today’s visit with Dr. Oefeleian was, unfortunately, far from a good experience.

After checking in, providing a urine sample, and speaking with the assistant who gathered information for the doctor, Dr. Oefeleian entered the room and asked, “What can I do for you today?” My wife began explaining why she had been referred, but before she could even finish her first sentence, he interrupted her with a dismissive “blah, blah, blah” type of response.

We tried to explain the situation and answer his questions, but he repeatedly interrupted before my wife could finish. He then asked why she thought she had a UTI. When she explained that the hospital had told her she had one, he interrupted again and stated that if she wasn’t experiencing certain symptoms, then she did not have a UTI and should not go to the hospital telling them she had one.

I understand and actually appreciate the point he appeared to be making about unnecessary antibiotics, over-treatment, and the potential consequences of repeatedly taking medications that may not be necessary. That is an important conversation to have. However, the way the information was delivered was the problem.

There was very little patience, compassion, or willingness to actually listen. At one point, my wife looked at me and said, “I think it’s time to leave.” I asked her to stay because I wanted to understand the doctor’s medical reasoning and give him the opportunity to explain what he was trying to communicate.

What was especially disappointing was that he never really engaged with my wife as a patient. He remained standing across the room, leaning against a counter, rather than approaching the examination table and having a professional conversation with her. He also emphasized that he was a surgeon and that he deals with important medical procedures—not UTI infections—and questioned what he could possibly do for her if she wasn’t experiencing symptoms.

Again, the medical point may have been legitimate. The delivery was not.

Patients deserve to be heard before being corrected. A physician can disagree with a patient’s understanding of their condition, explain why previous treatment may have been inappropriate, and educate them about when antibiotics are warranted—all without interrupting them, speaking dismissively, or making them feel like they’re wasting his time.

We are paying for a professional medical service. The least a patient should be able to expect is to be listened to carefully and treated with basic courtesy and respect.

I left this appointment feeling that my wife wasn’t being treated like a patient who deserved compassion and an explanation, but rather like an inconvenience.

I sincerely hope this review is taken as constructive feedback. Good medicine isn’t just about knowing the facts; it’s also about knowing how to communicate those facts to the person sitting in front of you.

one_star_reviews.text:
I rarely leave negative reviews, but I feel compelled to share my family's experience with Patricia Greco, NP-C, and Citrus Valley internal medicine so that others can make informed decisions regarding their healthcare.

My father was recovering from a leg amputation due to complications from advanced diabetes. At the time, he required dialysis three times per week, ongoing medication management, and transportation assistance to attend his treatments.

During a scheduled appointment, my family requested assistance with obtaining necessary diabetes and blood pressure medications, as well as help submitting a transportation authorization referral required by his insurance carrier. We were advised by Patricia Greco that she could not assist with certain medication and referral requests.

Because this did not seem consistent with what we had been told by the insurance company, I contacted the insurer directly. The insurance representative worked with the provider's office and informed me that the office had verbally agreed to submit the transportation authorization. Unfortunately, we later learned that the authorization was never submitted.

At the same time, my father's blood pressure medication was never received by the pharmacy despite it being discussed during the appointment. I personally contacted the pharmacy multiple times and made several attempts to reach Patricia Greco's assistant, Carolina. I left detailed voicemails requesting assistance and explaining the urgency of the situation, yet I never received a return call, update, or follow-up.

For a patient recovering from major surgery and relying on life-sustaining dialysis treatments, the lack of communication, follow-through, and urgency was extremely concerning. Our family felt abandoned during one of the most vulnerable periods of my father's recovery.

I understand that healthcare offices are busy and that mistakes can happen. However, when patients with serious medical needs are involved, timely communication and follow-through are essential. In our experience, those expectations were not met.

Based on our experience, I cannot recommend this provider or office. We felt that obtaining basic assistance required repeated phone calls, involvement from the insurance company, and significant self-advocacy during a time when our focus should have been on my father's recovery.

I hope this feedback encourages the office to improve its responsiveness, patient communication, and overall coordination of care so that other families do not experience similar challenges.

— Jesus Gonzalez
Concerned Family Member and Patient Advocate

My father in law was repeatedly telling staff that he could not breathe. His daughter was called and told that staff could not calm him down. By the time she arrived, he had called 911 himself from his cell phone because he was still struggling to breathe.

What made the situation worse was that a staff member told his daughter that she had spoken with a director and that he would not be welcome back if he left by ambulance because of the way he was acting and because he had called 911 himself.

He was not simply being difficult or agitated. He was transported to the hospital and found to be in acute hypoxic respiratory failure and suffering an NSTEMI. His condition was serious enough that he was intubated and placed on mechanical ventilation in the emergency department and then admitted to the ICU.

The hardest part for our family to accept is that he was repeatedly saying he could not breathe, yet the situation appeared to be treated primarily as a problem of calming him down. He ultimately had to call 911 himself.

We are also extremely troubled that calling 911 for emergency medical help was reportedly used as a reason to tell his daughter he would not be welcome back.

We have submitted a formal complaint regarding what happened. Based on our family’s experience, I cannot recommend this facility.

one_star_reviews.text: Horrible experience waited more than 9 hours to get a room and on top of that being in so much pain and a transplant patient

Extremely disappointing and unacceptable experience at the Cedars-Sinai Emergency Department.

We came to the ER with our 2-month-old baby after he had received his vaccinations three days earlier and began experiencing repeated episodes of severe crying and apparent abdominal pain. We explained this clearly during triage and repeatedly afterward.

We have now been sitting in an extremely crowded waiting room for approximately three hours, surrounded by dozens of sick patients, while our 2-month-old infant has still not been evaluated by a physician.

I understand completely that an emergency department must prioritize patients according to medical urgency, and I am not criticizing the doctors for treating genuinely critical patients first. My complaint is about the way we were treated by the staff while waiting.

I approached the nursing/reception area approximately six times simply asking for information or assistance. Instead of basic compassion or communication, we repeatedly received dismissive responses of “there is no update.”

My interactions with Dustin, RN, and Terrence Nelif, RN, were particularly upsetting. I asked for assistance multiple times and felt ignored and dismissed. At one point, I was speaking directly to a staff member who continued typing on the computer without even acknowledging me. I wasn’t demanding special treatment — I was a worried father asking someone to communicate with me about my 2-month-old baby.

We repeatedly explained our concern about keeping such a young infant for hours in an overcrowded ER waiting room surrounded by sick patients. Even if nothing could be done to shorten the wait, there are professional and compassionate ways to communicate that to frightened parents.

What made this experience particularly disturbing wasn’t simply the three-hour wait. It was the complete lack of empathy, communication, and basic human courtesy we experienced while waiting with an infant.

Parents bringing a 2-month-old baby to an emergency room are already scared. They should not have to repeatedly beg staff members simply to acknowledge them or explain what is happening.

Cedars-Sinai has an outstanding reputation, which is exactly why we came here. The treatment we experienced tonight from the front-line ER staff fell shockingly short of the standard I expected from this institution.

I sincerely hope Cedars-Sinai management reviews what happened tonight, including our interactions with the staff involved, because no family — especially one sitting in an emergency department with a 2-month-old infant — should be made to feel invisible or treated without basic dignity and compassion.

I had my CPAP orientation and after two nights of use, I realized this would not work for me. A day later (3 days after orientation), I called Lincare to return the CPAP. I was told that I am in a “trial period” and encouraged to try out a different mask instead. A few days later (1 week after orientation), I picked up a new mask. It did not work for me either, so I called again to return everything. I was then told I have 90 days to try out the CPAP machine before deciding.

I ended up finally returning the machine in person 35 days after my orientation; well before the 90 days that I was told about. Despite this, Lincare charged me for the machine, the second mask, and accessories, including duplicate charges for some items! Returning the equipment did not result in a refund! Charges continued even after the return, and I was eventually threatened with collections if I didn't pay. So out of pocket I had to pay around $500 for equipment I had asked to return within days of receiving.

Based on this experience, there is no “trial” period. As soon as you accept the equipment, you will be billed, including duplicate charges, regardless of whether you keep or return the equipment. So, ultimately, even if you know you will be 100% keeping the equipment, I recommend using a different company; at the very least to avoid duplicate charges.

What’s criminal about that (and that I worked with NPC coach before that) is that the training is really a random thought from coaches: they are not being proactive as far as understanding what one needs to improve. Example: I do weighted pull-ups with an additional 35 dumbbell, reps are within 8 to 12. I’m good at that. But I suck at abs. Yet, coaching meetups are random programs that are not a response to one’s weakness. And finally, the nail in(to) the coffin: nutrition. This is the profoundly disgusting part. California has some liability as far as giving recommendations for a diet. That is enlightening, given one cannot outtrain a bad diet. Instead, EOS relies on a machine to assess body composition, and does not take action to be personable with one’s diet. And they don’t look at your picture. I’ve worked with Oregon coaches in the past (Dan Simpson; notoriously), and they all ask for pictures to assess progress. This is how you get results. What EOS does is creating programs that do not reflect one’s areas of improvement. Training themselves  are great: they just do not align with a real progression plan. I feel scammed! I am disgusted!

one_star_reviews.text:
I am extremely frustrated and disappointed with my recent experiences with Sutter Health and the way my surgeries have been handled.

Two weeks ago, I wrote a review about receiving incorrect information from a pre-op nurse over the phone. Based on that information, I took a medication the morning of my scheduled surgery. As a result, the surgery center canceled my procedure just minutes before they were about to place an IV in my hand. I had to reschedule the surgery for a later date.

At the same time, I already had a second surgery—a spinal procedure—scheduled for a Thursday. As I was leaving my home to go to the surgery center, I received a call informing me that the anesthesiologist would not perform the surgery at the center and that it needed to be done in a hospital in case complications occurred. Once again, I was left with no choice but to reschedule.

I tried to roll with the punches and moved the first surgery to an earlier date. I was expecting to finally have that surgery next Tuesday. Then, once again, I received a call from a pre-op nurse informing me that the anesthesiologist now wanted additional testing, including an echocardiogram, before proceeding. Of course, I need a referral from my primary care physician, and getting an appointment and completing the test before the scheduled surgery date is practically impossible.

So, once again, my surgery is being delayed.

My spinal surgery is scheduled for next month, but at this point, I have very little confidence that it will actually happen as scheduled—even though it will now be performed in a hospital.

What is most frustrating is that these surgeries were presented to the surgery center well in advance. It is extremely difficult to understand why the anesthesia team is apparently reviewing cases so late in the process, sometimes only shortly before the scheduled procedure. If additional testing or a hospital setting is required, why isn't that determined weeks in advance? Patients should not have to rearrange their lives, prepare for surgery, fast, make transportation arrangements, deal with the stress and anxiety of surgery, and then find out at the last minute that the procedure cannot go forward.

Surgery is stressful enough without repeatedly being given conflicting information and having procedures canceled or delayed at the last minute. I understand that patient safety must come first, and I absolutely support appropriate medical precautions. However, better communication, earlier case review, and better coordination between the surgical team, anesthesiologists, pre-op nurses, and patients should be basic expectations.

I have been with Sutter Health for years, and most of my medical records and history are already within their system. Unfortunately, these experiences over the past several months have seriously damaged my confidence in the organization.

California State University system is offering Sutter Health as one of the options during upcoming open enrollment. Based on my recent experiences, it is very unlikely that I will choose Sutter, and I certainly cannot recommend the plan to my colleagues.

At this point, I am seriously considering requesting copies of all my medical records before the end of the year and moving my care elsewhere. Perhaps my new health plan will provide the level of communication, coordination, and patient care that I expected from Sutter but have not experienced over the past few months.

Patients deserve better than last-minute surprises when it comes to something as important and stressful as surgery.

one_star_reviews.text:
In March 2026, my son’s doctor prescribed a medically necessary, FDA-registered Cubby Bed because of his autism, severe headbanging, self-injurious behaviors, and serious nighttime safety needs. His OT also provided supporting documentation.

In May, New West Medical told me their mobility specialist would contact me for a home evaluation. That evaluation never happened, despite my repeated calls.

On June 30, I went there in person and was told Partnership had denied the bed. I contacted Partnership myself and learned New West had never even submitted the request.

On July 7, I confronted New West with what Partnership told me. They continued claiming the bed had been denied until I told them I knew they were not telling me the truth because I had spoken directly with Partnership.

The prescription was finally submitted on July 13. On July 23, I received an actual denial letter from Partnership. I immediately requested copies of everything New West had submitted regarding my son’s Cubby Bed.

That is when I discovered what appeared to be a false home evaluation dated June 5. Nobody from New West had ever come to my home to perform this evaluation. It described my two-story home as single-story, included measurements that were not from my home, claimed my son had his own room and was left unsupervised, and incorrectly described him as blind and deaf.

I filed a grievance, and Partnership later documented that New West had “misrepresented” information and confirmed that the reported home visit had not occurred.

Since sharing my experience publicly, multiple other people have come forward saying they experienced similar problems with New West involving other types of medical equipment—not just Cubby Beds. Based on my documented experience and what others are reporting, I have serious concerns that there may be a larger pattern involving New West and Medi-Cal equipment requests. I believe these practices need to be thoroughly investigated by the appropriate agencies.

Families should not have to investigate their own medical equipment provider to determine whether a medically necessary prescription was actually submitted or whether information submitted about their child is accurate.

If you deal with New West Medical, request copies of EVERYTHING they submit on your behalf and check every page carefully. Had I not requested those records, I may never have discovered what happened.

one_star_reviews.text:
Dr. Douglas Davies is a wonderful, thorough, and professional neurologist, and staff members like Eddie (who kindly offered to help book my MRI) and the curly-haired front desk representative were polite and welcoming. Unfortunately, my experience with another front desk employee—a woman with long, straight black hair—was unacceptable and deeply stressful.

I arrived at 3:45 PM for my 4:00 PM appointment on August 5. When handed intake paperwork, I politely asked to use the restroom first. Instead of showing basic courtesy, she told me with attitude: "You can go, but if you don’t fill these papers before the 10-minute grace time period, the doctor may or may not see you."

After rushing back from the restroom, I asked her to clarify, and when I asked if she was threatening to cancel my appointment, she repeated: "Fill these forms before the grace period of 10 minutes if you want to see the doctor."

This interaction highlighted major issues:

1. **Lack of Empathy:** She showed zero respect for a patient needing the restroom, ignoring that someone might have bladder issues or distress. Expecting a patient to ignore basic physical needs under threat of cancellation is completely unprofessional.
2. **Condescending Demeanor:** She spoke to me in a patronizing manner—like a principal threatening a child—and smirked repeatedly while insisting on the 4:10 PM deadline.
3. **Flawed Intake Notification:** Digital forms were never sent 2–3 days prior as reminders (the only link received was a month earlier on July 9 when I booked). The scheduler also failed to mention arriving 30 minutes early.
4. **Unrealistic Rushing:** Earlier at 1:40 PM, the clinic called asking if I could fill a last-minute 2:30 PM slot. Calling 50 minutes prior is unrealistic, and it felt like the front desk aggressively rushed me to make up for their open schedule slot.
5. **Double Standards on Time:** Under extreme pressure, I finished paperwork by 4:09 PM. Yet, I sat waiting until 4:27 PM before Eddie called me back, followed by another 10-minute wait in the exam room. It is hypocritical to threaten patients over minutes when the clinic itself runs nearly 30 minutes late.

Management needs to address front-desk professionalism. Patients visiting a neurology clinic should never be treated with condescension or threats when asking to use the restroom.

one_star_reviews.text:
I was referred to this doctor by my primary care physician for my menopausal symptoms, and I made this appointment approximately three and a half months ago at Chaparral Medical Center in Chino Hills. Today was finally supposed to be my appointment.

I never received a reminder call, text, or any notification that my appointment had been changed. Something told me this morning to call and confirm before making the trip. I’m very glad I did.

When I called, I was told that my appointment was actually scheduled for October 20th. I was completely unaware that I had been rescheduled. I was also told that the doctor is no longer seeing patients at the Chino Hills or Pomona locations and is now only seeing patients in Rancho Cucamonga.

My biggest concern is the lack of communication. How can a patient wait three and a half months for an appointment, be moved to a completely different date and location, and not be notified? If I had not called that morning, I would have shown up expecting to see the doctor and potentially been turned away.

After waiting this long, I decided that I don’t want to wait another month or continue with a medical office that handles appointments this way. I contacted my primary physician today and asked for a referral to a different endocrinologist.

Unfortunately, after reading the other reviews about patients experiencing canceled or changed appointments, long waits, and communication problems, my experience seems to be consistent with what others have reported.

I’m extremely disappointed. Patients shouldn’t have to chase down their own appointments to find out that they’ve been rescheduled without notice.

I lived at this complex for 10 years, and I would not recommend it. Although it is supposed to help low-income families, in my experience, it felt like they tried to take every extra penny you earned. If you worked overtime or got a part-time job to get ahead, your rent would increase. My rent seemed to go up about every six months with recertification, and some of the increases never felt clearly explained or legitimate.The former manager would drive around the complex every single day looking for anything residents might be doing People were so uncomfortable around her. I personally never had problems until the manager's relatives moved in. After I rejected unwanted attention from her sister's husband, I felt I was suddenly being targeted with pictures and complaints about things I was doing.
I also questioned why so many of the manager's relatives appeared to be living there and receiving favorable arrangements. On top of that, deliveries were always a issue because there was no call box or access for drivers to access the building.
If your income stays exactly the same, the program may work for you. But if you're trying to work extra hours or earn a little more money to improve your situation,  the rent would just keep increasing or even retro pay, after the property was sold to someone else the ones who actually benefited with money is the maintenance guy the manager and the the lady from the office.

I was beyond disappointed in how this was handled and how I was treated.
I lost almost everything I owned and thousands of dollars in the process.
It will take me years to physically, mentally, emotionally and financially recover from this.

one_star_reviews.text:
Under California law, what the landlord is doing is illegal.
Under Senate Bill 329 and the California Fair Employment and Housing Act (FEHA), Section 8 vouchers are classified as a protected "source of income". While a landlord can use an income multiplier (like requiring 2x income), state law explicitly requires that this ratio must be applied only to your tenant portion of the rent, not the total contract rent.
How the Law Applies to Your Example
Total Rent: $1,400
Required Multiplier: 2x
If your portion is $300: They can only require you to earn $600/month ($300 × 2), because the housing voucher covers the remaining $1,100.
Illegal Practice: Requiring you to make $2,800/month ($1,400 × 2) defeats the purpose of the voucher program and constitutes source-of-income discrimination under state law.
Steps You Can Take
1. Inform them of the law in writing: Send an email or message politely stating that under California FEHA (Government Code § 12955) and SB 329, income requirement multipliers for housing voucher holders must be calculated using only the tenant's individual portion of the rent.
2. Contact your local Public Housing Authority (PHA): Inform your Section 8 caseworker about the landlord's policy. PHAs often step in to educate landlords about compliance.
3. File a Fair Housing Complaint: You can file a complaint with the California Civil Rights Department (CRD) or reach out to a local Fair Housing organization (such as Central California Legal Services or the Fair Housing Council in your area) to report source-of-income discrimination.

one_star_reviews.text:
My family and I are devastated by the care my 75-year-old mother received following her surgery.

At her post-op appointment, her surgeon told us that she had an infection. My mom was elderly and immunocompromised, yet instead of sending her immediately to the ER for evaluation and treatment or starting antibiotics, she was sent back to rehab. We were then left waiting for more than a week for a CT scan to determine the cause of the infection.

During that week, my mom’s condition declined drastically. We watched her become weaker and sicker while we desperately tried to get answers and appropriate care. By the time more was done, the damage was devastating. My mom ultimately passed away.

As her daughter, I will always struggle with the fact that she was clearly fighting an infection and was sent back to rehab instead of receiving immediate medical attention. I will always wonder if things could have been different if her infection had been treated when it was first identified.

Our family trusted this surgeon to recognize the seriousness of my mom’s condition and act accordingly. We feel that she deserved more urgent attention, more thorough evaluation, and better care.

Losing my mom has left an unimaginable hole in our lives. Knowing that she was suffering while we were waiting for answers makes this loss even harder to carry. I hope no other family has to experience what ours did.

one_star_reviews.text:
DO NOT entrust Savant of Jurupa Valley with the wellbeing of your loved ones.

My parents were residents at Savant for 5 months beginning January 2026.

Both parents are in wheelchairs and need a high degree of assistance. Before moving in, Savant evaluated each to determine Individualized Care Plans, which Savant determined to be at the highest levels.  That alone should have guaranteed they would have adequate care and be safe.

My first indication of potential problems was finding rodent tape under the bathroom sink. By week two, I noticed a urine smell when I walked into the apartment due to several unbagged soiled diapers in various waste baskets. A few days later I found soiled linens and clothes mixed with regular laundry.  There were numerous incidents of wet towels being left on the bathroom floor, on top of the sink, and on dressers. The shower and toilet were rarely left clean. These are all violations of the California Residential Care Facilities Code of Regulations, Title 22.

Our contract included extensive hands-on support, they should have been safe. Instead, they had multiple “assisted falls” with two falls leading to emergency room visits.  After one of the falls, my father told the emergency room doctor that the person with him during a transfer from his bed to a chair, told him “You can do it yourself”.

After each incident, I immediately alerted and discussed the situation with management, who in the beginning apologized and assured me that they would be providing additional training and further communication with the care team. I repeatedly asked if there was something I could do or provide to ensure the incidents would no longer occur. The problems continued and one to two times per week I sent photos of soiled diapers, linens and clothes, as well as wet towels and unmade beds to the management team.  Eventually, management stopped responding to my concerns.

Management told me several times that they were short staffed.  Being short-staffed is never a residents’ concern and is not an excuse.  Staff shortages are instead caused by mismanagement and should be addressed immediately by additional hires and scheduling oversight. Considering the cost of living in an Assisted Living Community, it’s hard to believe staff shortages are a monetary issue.

The need to move my parents out of Savant at Jurupa Valley was apparent when I was told by management that staff was having “care burnout” due to the families’ concerns and that “the family needed to lower our expectations of care”.

Savant at Jurupa Valley isn’t a community that should be trusted with the care of your loved ones.
